# click

Third-party CLI framework for Python. Commands and options are declared as **decorators** on the
function that implements them, so the parser definition sits directly above the code it feeds.

## Where it is used

Lab 09 of [[python-programming-laboratories]] — a CSV reporting CLI over a 10,360-row dataset,
producing spreadsheet output via openpyxl and using [[factory-boy-and-faker]] for its test fixtures.

## Why it is here at all

Not because it was the best available option, but because the repo runs an explicit A/B: the core
`weblog` CLI uses [[argparse]] and this lab uses click, on comparable problems, on purpose. The
comparison and its verdict are recorded on [[click-versus-argparse]].

The short version of the trade-off as the repo states it: click's decorators are terser when a
command has a lot of flags; argparse's subparsers give more control over a command *hierarchy*.

## What the decorator style buys

- **`@click.option` / `@click.argument`** attach directly to the handler — no separate parser-building
  block to keep in sync with the signature.
- **Type conversion and validation are declarative**, including `click.Path(exists=True)`, so
  "this file must exist" is a parser concern rather than a first-line-of-the-function concern.
- Help text is derived from the same declaration, so it cannot drift from the parsing.

The cost is a dependency and a layer of magic between `sys.argv` and the function — which is exactly
why it lives in the optional `labs` extra rather than the dependency-free core. See
[[setuptools-and-pyproject]] and [[zero-dependency-no-build-step]].
